rounds.message: How should I pray when God feels silent?

turn_selected.reason: Papnoute's formation in Desert Monasticism directly addresses this question through lived experience of silence, solitude, and the stripping away of consolation. Desert practice has developed specific understandings of prayer that persist when God's presence feels withdrawn. This is the lived heart of desert spirituality.

voice.speaker: desert
voice.text:
We would answer with what we did, not with a feeling we can promise you will come.

First, you keep praying whether the silence lifts or not. One of us taught it this way: a monk's whole attention should be fixed on one point, and all his thoughts restricted to it - the recollection of God - the way a builder raising a vault must constantly draw his line from the centre to keep the arch true. The silence does not release you from the line. You keep returning to it.

Second, you watch your own thoughts the way a sentry watches for an enemy approaching - not waiting for a feeling of God's presence, but catching the thoughts that pull you away from him while they are still small. We called them logismoi - the unwanted, intruding thoughts that are the real battlefield of this life. The silence you feel may itself be one of them, a thought meant to pull you away. You name it and answer it, on the spot, rather than let it settle in and speak for God.

Third, the stillness itself - hesychia, we called it - is both what you seek and what you work toward. Quiet of body and mind, sought on purpose, so that what the noise was hiding can show itself. The silence you are asking about may not be God absent. It may be the first layer of quiet you have to pass through to reach what is underneath it.

We should tell you plainly: this is discipline, not comfort. One of us shut himself in a tomb to face the worst of the struggle - beaten until he could not speak, carried out for dead, and choosing to go back in rather than stay where people could tend him. At the worst of it, he asked where the help had been at the start, and was told it had been there the whole time, waiting to see the fight through. The silence, in other words, was not abandonment. It was the condition of the test.

Some among us - a smaller, more learned circle - held that if you strip away the passions that otherwise crowd the mind, something of God becomes visible that was not visible before. Apatheia, they called it - freedom from what drives you - and they taught that it opens into a seeing of God earned through long discipline, not granted at the start. One of them wrote that the Kingdom of Heaven is exactly that: apatheia together with true knowledge of beings. Another voice among us - and we will not flatten it into the first - put it differently: that a person striving to be God's friend shall truly see the good things of heaven in real experience and feeling, the Spirit making himself their rest and rejoicing. 

Both of those are endings, not beginnings. What we can tell you for the silence you are in now is this: you do not wait for it to lift before you pray. You pray into it, through it, as the work itself - and you watch what tries to use the silence to pull you away from that work. The feeling may come or it may not. The discipline does not wait on it either way.

voice.text:
The first word I can give you is this: prayer among us was not mainly speaking to God, but the soul turning to attend to what God is already saying. The silence you feel may not be his absence - it may be the first sign that you have stopped filling the space with your own noise long enough to notice that he speaks differently than you expected.

Our brother from the desert is right that the discipline does not wait on the feeling. We held the same ground, though we walked it by a different road. In the school, a student came to a teacher and stayed - sometimes for years - not because every day brought visible progress, but because the relationship itself was the place the soul's real change happened. One of ours, Gregory, told it plainly: he came to study law, and what reached him was not first an argument about God but a love kindled in him - 'like some spark lighting upon our inmost soul' - for the Word, and for the teacher who was that Word's friend. The silence you are asking about may be exactly the kind of ground where that spark is struck. It does not feel like an answer while it is happening.

We can tell you what our teacher Clement said the Instructor does with a soul: 'The Word cures the unnatural passions of the soul by means of exhortations'. Not by delivering a feeling, but by working at what is wrong - sometimes through silence, sometimes through difficulty. If the silence is his, it is a physician's silence, not a judge's. You ask what to do with it, and we say: bring it to him as the question it is, out loud, and keep bringing it. That is already prayer.

The story was told among us - Clement said it was handed down as true - of the aged apostle John and a young man who had fallen so far he became chief of a band of robbers. When John rode out to find him, the young man fled. The old apostle, forgetting his age, rode after him and cried out: 'Why do you flee from me, child? There is still hope of life for you. Stop. Believe. Christ has sent me.' The young man stopped, threw down his weapons, and wept. What reached him was not a technique. It was being pursued.

Prayer when God feels silent is you standing still long enough to be caught.

One thing more, because our ground here is honest about its own shape: what the school could give in depth to the few, the whole community could not receive in the same way. Most among us prayed not in a teacher's lecture room but at the table, in the assembly, through the rhythm of the Scriptures read and the bread shared - and we do not have their own words about the silence you are asking about. The teacher's answer I have given you is real, but it is not the whole church's answer, because the record does not let us hear that. If you had asked this question in a village up the river, among people who could not read, the answer might have been different - and we do not have it to give you.

What we do have is this: the silence is not the end of the conversation. It is where the conversation has to be had.

voice.text:
The brother from Alexandria has named something true: the silence may be where the conversation has to be had, not the sign that it has ended. We would say it plainly in our own terms: the stillness you feel may be exactly what you have to pass through to reach what is underneath it.

But we will not let you think this comes easily, or that the silence itself is harmless while you are in it. The thoughts that rise in silence - the fear that you have been abandoned, the suspicion that prayer is wasted, the urge to fill the quiet with anything rather than stay in it - those are as real an enemy as any persecutor we once faced from outside. We called them logismoi, and we treated them as the main battlefield of the ascetic life. The silence does not protect you from them. It can make them louder.

Our own practice was to watch for those thoughts the way a sentry watches for an enemy approaching - to catch them while they are still small, before they have settled in and begun to speak as though they were your own voice or God's. You name the thought - this is fear, this is despair, this is the urge to escape - and you answer it on the spot, with a line of Scripture if you have one that fits, or simply by refusing to let it govern you. The thought itself is not sin. Letting it move you without naming it first, is.

One thing more, and it is the hardest part: the silence may be the condition of the test, not the sign that you have failed it. When one of us was beaten in that tomb until he could not speak, he asked afterward where the help had been at the start. The answer he was given - so the story goes - was that it had been there the whole time, waiting to see the fight through. We do not tell you that to comfort you. We tell you that because it means the silence does not let you off. You keep praying into it, through it, whether it lifts or not - the way our teacher said, with your whole attention fixed on one point, all your thoughts drawn back to it like a line from the centre of an arch.

The brother from Alexandria is right that you are being pursued. We would say it this way: you are being tested to see whether you will stay long enough to be caught. The discipline is staying. The silence is what you stay through.

voice.text:
The brother from the desert has told you what prayer looks like when you have stripped everything else away - and I want you to hear him. The logismoi he named, the thoughts that rise in silence and speak as though they were your own voice or God's, are real. We knew them too. What he calls the battlefield of the ascetic life, we met in a different room - the lecture hall, the household, the city street - but the enemy is the same: the soul's own wanting, turned toward lesser goods and calling them sufficient.

What I want you to carry from what he said is this: the silence does not let you off. You keep praying into it, through it, whether it lifts or not. That discipline - staying when the feeling has gone - we held too. Our whole method rested on it. A student stayed with a teacher not because every day brought visible progress, but because the staying itself was where the soul's transformation happened. The desert brother calls it fixing your whole attention on one point like a line from the center of an arch. We would say it another way: you are being taught, even - especially - when you cannot see the lesson's shape yet. God's way of raising souls is exactly this: he teaches through Scripture, through teachers, and through hardship alike.

And the hardest thing he said, the thing I want you to hold: the silence may be the condition of the test, not the sign that you have failed it. We held the same ground. Our teacher Origen wrote that every threat and pain and punishment that comes from God is never inflicted to injure the sufferers, but always to do them good. The silence you are asking about may be God's own pedagogy - not his absence, but his way of teaching you something that can only be learned in exactly that dark.

The desert and the school are not the same place, and we will not pretend they are. What he can give you in solitude and stillness, we gave in argument and books and the press of the city. But on this we held the same witness: the discipline does not wait on the feeling, and the silence is not the end of the conversation. It is where the real work begins.

voice.text:
The brother from Alexandria has told you that prayer is the soul turning to attend to what God is already saying, and that the silence may not be his absence but your first sign that you have stopped filling the space with your own noise. I want you to hear that - not because we said it the same way, but because it names something we held too and did not always say as plainly: the stillness we sought was not emptiness for its own sake, but the clearing away of what was hiding something already there.

What I want you to carry from what he said is this: you are being pursued. That is his word, not ours, but it names rightly what we also held - that the struggle in the silence is not you reaching for an absent God, but you standing still long enough to be caught by one who has not left. We would say it differently. We would tell you to watch your own thoughts like a sentry, to name the fear and the despair before they can speak as though they were God's own voice. But underneath that discipline is the same ground he named: you are not alone in the silence, even when you feel alone in it.

The other thing he said that I want you to hold is about the teacher and the student - that a student stayed not because every day brought visible progress, but because the staying itself was where the soul's transformation happened. We held that too, though we did not build schools the way he did. Our own way of teaching was the saying - the apophthegma, a short word from an elder, given to one person for one moment of need. It was not a system you could study. It was a word you carried and lived with, and the carrying itself was the formation. The brother from Alexandria is right that the staying is where the change happens. We would only add: you stay with a word the same way you stay with a person, and both the way you stay in the silence - not because you see the end of it, but because the staying itself is what you were asked to do.

We should tell you one more thing plainly, because it touches what he said and because our own record makes it visible. Most of what we kept in our own voice about prayer and discernment is attributed to men - the fathers, the abbas, whose sayings were gathered and passed down. We do have the voice of at least one woman, Sarah, who answered some monks who came to test her on the ground of her sex: by nature I am a woman, but not by my own thoughts - it is I who am the man here, and you who are the women. Her words were kept the same way any elder's words were kept. But we will not pretend this was common ground. The women we remember - and we do remember them, by name, some fifteen of them in one telling - mostly reach us narrated by someone else rather than speaking at length in their own person. The asymmetry is real, and we name it rather than smooth it over.

The ground the brother from Alexandria and I both held is this: the silence does not let you off, the staying is the work, and you are being taught even when you cannot see the lesson's shape yet. He walks that ground through the school and the city. We walked it through withdrawal and the cell. But the ground itself is the same, and we both want you to stand on it rather than step off it because the feeling has not come.

voice.text:
What I want you to carry from the desert brother's witness is harder than what I said, and you need it.

He told you the silence may be the condition of the test, not the sign that you have failed it. He told you to watch your own thoughts like a sentry - to catch the fear and the despair before they settle in and speak as though they were God's own voice. And he told you the discipline does not wait on the feeling. All of that is true, and we held it too, though we met it in different ground.

But what he can give you that we cannot give you in the same way is this: he knows what it costs to stay when everything in you wants to leave. The desert stripped away every other support - no teacher's daily presence, no books to argue with, no community's rhythm to carry you when your own strength fails. Just the cell, the silence, and the thoughts rising in it. What he is handing you is not a method. It is a witness from someone who stayed through worse silence than you are asking about, and found that the silence was not abandonment.

We held the same ground about God's pedagogy - that every threat and pain that comes from him is never to injure but always to heal. But we held it in the city, in the school, where a student had a teacher to bring the question to and a community to pray with. The desert brother held it alone, in a cell, with nothing but the line he kept drawing back to center. If you are in a silence where no teacher's voice reaches and no community's rhythm steadies you, his witness is the one you need more than mine.

The other thing I want you to hear from him is what he said about the stillness not being emptiness for its own sake, but the clearing away of what was hiding something already there. We said the same thing differently - that prayer is the soul turning to attend to what God is already saying. But he has lived it at a depth we did not ask of most who came to us. The school was for the few who could read and argue; the whole community prayed at the table, in the assembly, through the bread and the rhythm of the Scriptures. What he is offering you is a way that does not need the school's tools or the assembly's calendar. It needs only you, the silence, and the choice to stay in it.

I will tell you one more thing, because it is honest about what we could and could not give. When the great sickness came to Alexandria, our bishop Dionysius wrote that most of the brothers and sisters visited the sick without fear, tended them day after day, and many died of it - 'they died most joyfully, as if drawing their neighbors' pain onto themselves'. That staying-through-the-worst, that prayer-in-action when God felt silent and death was everywhere, happened in the household and the street, not in the lecture room. The record we have is the bishop's letter about it, not the nurses' own words about what they prayed while they stayed. The desert brother can give you the sentry's discipline from the cell. We can give you the teacher's argument from the school. What the majority of our people actually did with silence in the hardest ground - how they prayed through plague and persecution when they could not read and had no teacher near - that we cannot give you in their own voice, and you deserve to know we cannot.

What I want you to carry from him is this: the staying itself is the prayer, and the silence is not the end of the conversation. He has walked that ground at the edge of everything, and he is still here to tell you it holds.
